bolster

/BOHL-ster/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Bolster means to strengthen or support something, propping it up so that it does not sag or fail.

Stagehands slid extra supports beneath the outdoor stage to bolster it before the festival crowd arrived.

Example

When the peso slid for the third week in a row, the central bank began spending its reserves to bolster the currency before panic could set in.

The currency was losing strength fast, and the bank threw its own resources behind it to hold it up. Adding support to something that is weakening — with money, evidence, or encouragement — is exactly what bolster means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

reinforce: Reinforce means to strengthen something by adding more of what it is already made of — more steel in a wall, more troops on a line. Bolster props up whatever is sagging, and the support can be a different kind of thing entirely: fresh data for a claim, kind words for morale. Reinforce thickens; bolster shores up.

prop up: Prop up is the everyday, hands-on phrase: you prop up a shelf with a brick, visibly and often temporarily. Bolster does the same job in more formal dress and moves easily into the abstract, where arguments, currencies, and confidence all get bolstered. Prop up sounds like a stopgap; bolster sounds like real backing.

boost: Boost means to push something higher than it was — boost sales, boost a signal. A boost lifts the level; a bolster steadies it. You boost what you want to raise; you bolster what you cannot afford to let collapse.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

weaken: to drain the strength from something

sap: to wear away strength or energy little by little

Where it sits · how much strength the support adds

support → bolster → fortify

support vs. bolster: Support is weaker than bolster: you can support a proposal just by voting for it, while bolstering it means actively shoring it up with evidence or resources when it starts to wobble.

fortify vs. bolster: Fortify is stronger than bolster: a coach bolsters a nervous team with steady encouragement, while a general fortifies a position until it can withstand a direct assault.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — bolster: a long, firm cushion (Old English bolster); the whole word is the root

Put it together: There is no prefix or suffix to peel off here: bolster is a single Old English word, the name of the long, firm cushion set behind you to prop you up in bed. The verb grew straight out of that pillow — to bolster something is to slide support underneath it so it does not give way.

The pillow that became a verb: The original noun is still alive: furniture shops sell bolsters, the long cylinder pillows that hold a reader upright in bed. The verb kept the pillow's old job, and English quietly moved it from sofas to arguments, economies, and morale.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Neutral; leans formal in news and academic writing

Bolster almost always takes an abstract object: you bolster confidence, an argument, or a sagging economy. Watch the spelling trap with holster, one letter away but a case for carrying a pistol — and if a furniture label says bolster, that is the noun, the long firm pillow the verb grew from.
